```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidymodels)
library(tidyverse)
library(mgcv)
source(here::here("R/theme.R"))
source(here::here("R/data.R"))
```

## Why this matters

Everything up to here has produced numbers. A paper needs sentences, and the step between
them is where most of the damage is done — not by people who do not understand their model,
but by people who understand it and then describe it in the vocabulary a reviewer expects.

This page takes the survey through the whole course, writes out the two paragraphs, and then
does the more useful thing: lists the claims we cannot make, and demonstrates the one kind of
error that no amount of validation will catch.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The analysis, in one place

Each step points at where it was argued for.

```{r}
#| label: pipeline
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()          # §2: raw -> clean, every decision as code

modelling <- survey |>
  select(abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3, salinity_psu,
         substrate, season, longitude, latitude) |>
  drop_na()

model_formula <- abundance ~ s(depth_m, k = 8) + s(temperature_c, k = 8) +
  s(chlorophyll_mg_m3, k = 8) + s(longitude, latitude, k = 30) +
  substrate + season + salinity_psu

set.seed(9)
folds <- vfold_cv(modelling, v = 10)           # §7: same folds for every model compared

pooled <- map_dfr(folds$splits, \(split) {
  fitted <- gam(model_formula, family = nb(), data = analysis(split))
  held   <- assessment(split)
  tibble(truth = held$abundance,
         prediction = as.numeric(predict(fitted, held, type = "response")))
})                                             # §7: pool out-of-fold predictions

final <- gam(model_formula, family = nb(), data = modelling)

tibble(`cross-validated RMSE` = rmse_vec(pooled$truth, pooled$prediction),
       `cross-validated R²`   = rsq_vec(pooled$truth, pooled$prediction),
       `mean-only baseline RMSE` = rmse_vec(modelling$abundance,
                                            rep(mean(modelling$abundance), nrow(modelling)))) |>
  mutate(across(everything(), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

The `s(longitude, latitude)` term is there because §6 found spatial structure that no
covariate explains; the negative binomial because §6 found the counts over-dispersed; the
smooth terms because §3 and §10 found the responses humped; and the model family because
[the comparison on page 3](black-box-or-not.qmd) put it ahead of a random forest and a
boosted tree on these folds.

## The Methods paragraph

> Abundance was modelled as a function of depth, bottom temperature, chlorophyll
> concentration, salinity, substrate type and season using a generalised additive model with
> a negative-binomial response (`mgcv` 1.9.4, R 4.6.1). Depth, temperature and chlorophyll
> entered as thin-plate smooths with a basis dimension of 8, and an isotropic smooth of
> longitude and latitude (basis dimension 30) was included to absorb spatial structure not
> explained by the covariates. Predictive performance was assessed by ten-fold
> cross-validation with out-of-fold predictions pooled before scoring, and the same folds
> were used for every candidate model compared. Three alternatives — a random forest, a
> gradient-boosted tree ensemble and a negative-binomial GLM with quadratic terms — were
> fitted for comparison and are reported in the supplement. Analysis code, the package
> lockfile and the cleaning script are archived at [DOI]; all random seeds are set in the
> code.

Every clause there is either a decision the course argued for or a number a reader can check.
Note what it does *not* contain: no claim that the model was "validated", no accuracy figure
without a baseline, and no silence about the models that lost.

## The Results paragraph

```{r}
#| label: results-numbers
summary(final)$s.table |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "smooth term") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) signif(x, 3)))
```

```{r}
#| label: results-parametric
summary(final)$p.table |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "term") |>
  filter(str_detect(term, "substrate|salinity")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

> The model explained substantially more variation than a no-skill baseline
> (cross-validated RMSE 4.08 against 4.82 for predicting the survey mean; cross-validated
> R² 0.28). Bottom temperature was the strongest predictor, with a clearly non-linear effect
> (4.6 effective degrees of freedom, $\chi^2$ = 116, $p < 0.001$) peaking at approximately
> 8 °C. Chlorophyll concentration had a positive effect that the model resolved as linear on
> the log scale (1.0 e.d.f., $p = 0.011$). Substrate type was associated with abundance,
> which was lower on rock than on gravel (−0.48 ± 0.18 on the log scale, $p = 0.007$) and on
> sand (−0.24 ± 0.11, $p = 0.029$); mud did not differ detectably from gravel. The spatial
> smooth was retained with 10.7 effective degrees of freedom ($p = 0.002$), indicating
> structure the measured covariates do not account for. Salinity showed no detectable effect
> (0.06 ± 0.12, $p = 0.60$). Depth showed a weak unimodal tendency peaking near 50 m that was
> not statistically distinguishable from no effect ($p = 0.061$); we do not interpret it
> further, for the reason given below.

Four things that paragraph does deliberately. It gives the baseline next to the score. It
reports the *shape* of the temperature effect, not only its significance. It reports salinity's
null result rather than omitting it. And it declines to interpret depth.

## The claims we cannot make

This is the section most papers do not have, and it is the one this course has spent ten
sections earning.

**We cannot claim a depth optimum.** The true optimum is at 80 m. The GAM's smooth peaks at
52 m, the random forest's partial dependence declines monotonically, and a GLM given the
generator's exact functional form estimates the depth quadratic at a fourteenth of its true
value. [Depth and temperature are confounded by the sampling design](partial-effects.qmd):
there are almost no cold shallow stations and almost no warm deep ones. No model can separate
them, and the honest sentence is *"the survey does not separate the effects of depth and
temperature"*.

**We cannot claim chlorophyll is or is not important.** The GAM finds it significant at
$p = 0.011$; permutation importance puts it inside the noise band on one split and first on
another, [swinging from rank 1 to rank 11 across eight splits](feature-importance.qmd),
because depth and season between them reconstruct most of it.

**We cannot claim anything causal.** The model is a description of how abundance co-varies
with what happened to be measured, on the stations that happened to be visited. That the
temperature effect nearly matches the generator here is a fact about a world we wrote.

**We cannot claim it will transfer.** The
[conformal coverage on page 5](communicating-uncertainty.qmd) dropped from 96% to 86% when the
model was calibrated on low-chlorophyll stations and asked about high-chlorophyll ones, with
no change in the interval width to warn us. Outside the sampled envelope there is no
guarantee, and §6 says the same about the model itself.

**We cannot report the uncertainty the software prints.** Seven models were compared before
this one was chosen, so the intervals above are conditional on a selection step they do not
account for ([§7](../07-validation/cross-validation.qmd)).

## The error validation cannot catch

Every safeguard in this course compares a model against the data. If the data itself is
biased, all of them pass.

Dredges and grabs catch poorly on hard substrate; this is a well-known gear effect, not a
hypothetical one. Suppose our gear recovered only half the animals present on rock. The
recorded counts on rock would be halved, everything else unchanged.

```{r}
#| label: observation-bias
set.seed(77)
biased <- modelling |>
  mutate(abundance = if_else(substrate == "rock", rbinom(n(), abundance, 0.5), abundance))

compare <- function(data, label) {
  set.seed(9)
  out_of_fold <- map_dfr(vfold_cv(data, v = 10)$splits, \(split) {
    fitted <- gam(model_formula, family = nb(), data = analysis(split))
    held   <- assessment(split)
    tibble(truth = held$abundance,
           prediction = as.numeric(predict(fitted, held, type = "response")))
  })
  full <- gam(model_formula, family = nb(), data = data)
  tibble(dataset = label,
         `CV RMSE` = rmse_vec(out_of_fold$truth, out_of_fold$prediction),
         `CV R²`   = rsq_vec(out_of_fold$truth, out_of_fold$prediction),
         `rock effect` = coef(full)[["substraterock"]],
         `std. error`  = sqrt(diag(vcov(full)))[["substraterock"]])
}

bind_rows(compare(modelling, "as recorded"),
          compare(biased, "gear halves the catch on rock")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

The estimated rock effect more than doubles, from −0.48 to −1.16. On the count scale that is
the difference between "rock holds about 38% fewer animals than gravel" and "rock holds about
69% fewer" — and the second sentence is the one that would be written up, with a $p$ value of
well under 0.001 behind it.

Now look at the validation columns. The biased model **scores better on both**:
cross-validated RMSE 4.008 against 4.079, R² 0.297 against 0.284. Not a warning anywhere —
a modest improvement.

That is not a fluke, it is structural. Cross-validation asks whether the model predicts the
data, and the biased model predicts the biased data very well. The held-out fold carries the
same bias as the training folds. There is no resampling scheme, no metric and no
interpretation method in this course that detects it.

::: {.callout-important}
**The only defences against observation bias are outside the model.** Knowing your gear's
catchability by substrate. Comparing against an independent method — video, acoustics, a
different net. Reporting the effort and the gear alongside the result so a reader can apply
their own correction. A model that reproduces biased survey data reproduces the bias, with
excellent validation statistics, and says nothing at all about it.
:::

## Before you submit

The reporting checklist is on [the reproducibility page](reproducibility.qmd). Three questions
to add to it, all of which this page has answered for the survey:

1. **What is my baseline?** A score without one is not a result.
2. **Which of my claims is not identified by my design?** Write that sentence down before a
   reviewer writes it for you.
3. **How would my data be biased if my method were imperfect, and would I be able to tell?**

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- Write the **baseline next to the score**, the **shape** of an effect rather than only its
  significance, and the **null results** rather than omitting them.
- List the claims the design does not support. On this survey that is the depth optimum,
  chlorophyll's importance, anything causal, and transfer beyond the sampled envelope.
- Uncertainty after a model search is wider than the software prints, because the search is
  not in the interval.
- **Observation bias is invisible to validation.** Halving the recorded catch on rock more
  than doubled the estimated rock effect and *improved* the cross-validated RMSE and R².
- The defences against that are gear calibration, an independent method, and transparent
  reporting of effort — not a better model.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Bias the data the other way — suppose the gear over-counts in high chlorophyll because of
   fouling — and check whether cross-validation notices. Then check whether the
   chlorophyll smooth changes sign.
2. Write the Results paragraph for the random forest instead. Which of the five sentences can
   you still write, and what do you have to replace them with?
